statement: Each square of a 2-row, 3-column grid holds a stack of at least one cube. The pictures show the stacks from the front and from the right. How many cubes are there?

figure.alt: Two views of the stacks. From the front: three columns of cubes, 2, 3 and 1 cubes tall from left to right. From the right: two columns, 1 and 3 cubes tall from left to right.

choices.misconception: I counted only the cubes in the front view, $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$, as if all the stacks stood in one row.
I put the front view in the tall row and only one cube in the short row, forgetting that every square has at least one cube.
I added the cubes in the two views, $6 + 4 = 10$, but some cubes appear in both views.
I copied the front view into both rows, $2 \times 6 = 12$, which makes the short row too tall for the view from the right.

hints: Start with the view from the right. What does it tell you about each row?
One row is never taller than 1 cube, and every square has a cube, so you know that row exactly. Then use the front view to work out the stacks in the other row.

The short row has 1 cube on each square: 3 cubes. The front columns of 2 and 3 must be stacks in the tall row, and the column that is 1 tall has 1 cube there too. So the tall row has $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$ cubes, and the total is $3 + 6 = 9$.

solutions.reliable: From the right, one row is 1 cube tall and the other is 3 tall. In the short row every square has at least one cube but no stack is taller than 1, so it has exactly 1 cube on each square: 3 cubes. From the front the columns are 2, 3 and 1 tall. The short row only reaches 1, so the stacks of 2 and 3 must be in the tall row. In the last column both stacks are 1 tall. So the tall row has 2, 3 and 1 cubes: 6 cubes. Total: $3 + 6 = 9$. The transferable idea: start with the view that pins down a whole row, then let the other view fill in the rest.

whyOnTest: Views of a solid test whether you can rebuild the stacks from two flat pictures and see which cubes each view hides.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
